Para sumar y restar se usa la forma binó: To add and subtract, the rectangular form is used: the real and imaginary parts are added (it is the parallelogram rule). To multiply and divide, the polar form is more convenient:
En binómica, el producto se hace como el: In rectangular form, the product is done like that of two binomials using $i^2 = −1$, and the quotient by multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, $z̄ = a − bi$, because $z z̄ = a^2 + b^2$ is real.

Un complejo distinto de cero tiene exact: A nonzero complex number has exactly n nth roots, all with the same modulus and spaced every 360°/n, at the vertices of a regular polygon:
Con los complejos, toda ecuación $a z^2: With complex numbers, every equation $a z^2 + b z + c = 0$ has two solutions, $z = {−b ± √Δ}/{2a}$. If the coefficients are real and $Δ = b^2 − 4ac < 0$, the solutions are complex conjugates, because $√Δ = i √(−Δ)$.
La exponencial de z = a + bi es e<sup>z<: The exponential of z = a + bi is e<sup>z</sup> = e<sup>a</sup>(cos b + i sin b): it has modulus e<sup>a</sup> and argument b, and repeats every 2πi. That is why the logarithm has infinitely many values, ln z = ln|z| + i(θ + 2kπ); the principal one is the one with −π < θ ≤ π. With it, powers with complex exponent are defined, z<sup>w</sup> = e<sup>w ln z</sup>: for example, i<sup>i</sup> = e<sup>−π/2</sup> is a real number.
Una ecuación polinómica de grado n tiene: A polynomial equation of degree n has exactly n complex solutions, counting repeated ones (fundamental theorem of algebra). The rational ones are found with Ruffini's rule among the divisors of the constant term, and if the coefficients are real, the complex ones come in conjugate pairs. In the plane, |z − a| = r is the circle with center a and radius r, |z − a| < r its interior, Re z > c a half-plane and |z − a| = |z − b| the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining a and b.
